page_summary:
The Earthshaker: Novel Outline is the canonical works record for PKD's primary text. It preserves a single archive manifestation and gives the work a stable bibliographic home. The preserved item here is The Earthshaker: Novel Outline (Unknown). The archive copy runs 2 pages.

Archive summary: Wanderer Miracle Child Benji The Earthshaker (Coming) Ch 1 the wanderer returns to his village.

Researchers can use this entry to trace publication context, later commentary, and relationships to other works.

structure.form: a 25-chapter outline in three named movements -- '(Coming),' '(Being),' and an implied resolution/descent -- tracking a mythic quest narrative rather than a scene-by-scene plot
movements: '(Coming)': a wanderer returns to his village and its miraculous child; he meets Benjie, the earth woman, amid a sense of impending, unspecified 'change.'

'(Being)': the man's backstory and ideals are given by flashback, and a group called 'the sown' undertakes a multi-chapter quest through world-mythological and esoteric traditions (Faust, gnosis, Cabala, astrology, mysticism, philosophy, the Magi) to find a serpent, eventually located near a Yggdrasil-like tree.

An implied resolution/descent: a message is delivered, the woman flees and hides, a fraught union of 'faith and reason' occurs between the man and woman, a symbolic death and birth are anticipated, and the woman ultimately departs as a self-directed 'Ulysses' figure rather than remaining.
structure.point_of_view: not determinable from the surviving outline, which is written in bare chapter-note shorthand rather than narrated prose.
structure.central_device: A syncretic quest structure that treats world mythology, world religion, and Western esotericism (Norse myth, Kabbalah, Faust, astrology, Homer) as interchangeable resources to be consulted in sequence toward a single unifying revelation, rather than as distinct traditions in tension with one another.

characters.name: The wanderer / the man
characters.note: Described only through his 'ideals,' a 'grandfather' connection to 'the sown,' and a chapter devoted to his early life via flashback -- the outline gives him thematic weight (faith, reason, leadership) without any concrete biographical or physical detail.

characters.name: Benjie, the earth woman
characters.note: Explicitly named as an elemental or symbolic 'earth woman' rather than an ordinary character; her arc runs from domestic partner to prostitute-figure to a Ulysses-like departing agent, suggesting a planned trajectory from grounded domesticity to autonomous, mythic self-determination.

characters.name: The sown
characters.role: a collective or lineage, possibly hidden or awakening
characters.note: Never clearly defined in the surviving fragments -- possibly a secret spiritual lineage or 'seed' group tied to the grandfather figure -- and referred to with the outline's own uncertainty ('not known is grandfather to ready??').

settings.name: The village and 'the road'
settings.note: Rendered only in the barest outline terms, as the site of the wanderer's return and of an approaching, unspecified 'change' or 'movement,' without further physical description.

settings.name: The woods, the serpent, and the tree
settings.note: The outline's clearest concrete image -- a serpent and tree 'found by chance' during a walk in the woods, explicitly likened to Yggdrasil, positioning the discovery as the quest's central mythic-religious object.

motifs: A syncretic quest through multiple world-religious and esoteric traditions in sequence (Faust, gnosis, Cabala, astrology, mysticism, philosophy, the Magi) toward a single revelation
A serpent and world-tree, explicitly compared to Yggdrasil, as the quest's central sacred object
An unresolved union of 'faith and reason' framed as 'a union of opposites not combined,' left as open conflict rather than synthesis
A female figure moving from domestic partner to prostitute to autonomous, self-directed departure, framed through the classical allusion to Ulysses
reading.significance: As a bare, unfinished outline rather than a completed work, this document's chief value is evidentiary: it shows Dick, at some undated point, sketching a mythic-religious quest narrative that deliberately blends Norse myth (Yggdrasil), Kabbalah, Faustian legend, astrology, and classical epic (Ulysses) into a single syncretic search structure -- a pattern of world-mythological synthesis strongly consistent with his post-1974 Exegesis-era thinking, though nothing in the surviving fragments allows a firm date or a connection to any specific published novel. Its telegraphic, self-questioning notation style (visible in bracketed uncertainties like 'not known is grandfather to ready??' and the outline's own closing 'x?') captures Dick's private, unfinished working process rather than any authorial statement intended for a reader, making it closer in kind to a planning document than to any other class of primary-source material in this corpus.
reading.closing_note: The outline ends on its own unresolved fragment -- 'The circle comp. Will found. x?' -- leaving unclear whether this marks an intended ending, a note to self about a still-undetermined resolution, or simply where the surviving document breaks off.

pkd_on_this_work.summary: This entire document is Dick's own private working notes; there is no separate 'commentary on it' to distinguish from the work itself.

evidence.quote: the serpent and tree found by chance. Walk in woods. Yggdrasil.
evidence.reading: The outline's clearest single image, and its only unambiguous connection to a specific named mythological tradition.

open_questions: Is there any external documentation (letters, Exegesis references, Sutin's or other biographers' accounts) dating this outline or connecting it to a specific period of Dick's career?
Was any portion of this outline's material -- the serpent-and-tree quest, the 'faith and reason' union, the sown -- absorbed into a published novel or into the Exegesis under different names?
Does 'JWH' refer to a specific intended meaning (a transliteration of the Tetragrammaton, YHWH?) and if so, how does that reshape the outline's religious framing?

reading_provenance.note: Close reading of the primary text plus attributed evidence from the archive. Candidate: not yet promoted to canonical.

critical_caution: This is a raw, telegraphic chapter outline for an apparently unwritten or unfinished novel -- not finished prose, and not fiction that can be synthesized into a plot summary in the ordinary sense. The surviving text is fragmentary shorthand (abbreviations, crossed-out words, bracketed uncertainties) rather than connected sentences, and no external documentation of this project's date, completion status, or eventual fate was found in this evidence pass. The 'reading' fields below describe what the outline's fragments suggest about a planned narrative, not a confirmed finished work; treat every claim here as inferential.
